elements.name: Lexer
elements.what: A component that converts a raw character stream into a stream of classified tokens (identifiers, literals, operators), usually via maximal-munch matching driven by a finite automaton or hand-written switch.
elements.problem: Parsing directly over characters entangles grammar logic with whitespace, comments, and literal syntax; a separate tokenization stage gives the parser a clean, higher-level symbol stream.
elements.named_in: Compilers: Principles, Techniques, and Tools (Dragon Book) - Aho, Lam, Sethi, Ullman (2006, 2nd ed.)

elements.name: Recursive Descent Parser
elements.what: A top-down parser written as a set of mutually recursive procedures, one per grammar nonterminal, each consuming the tokens its rule derives.
elements.problem: Table-driven parsing machinery is heavyweight and opaque; mapping grammar rules directly onto call structure yields a parser that is hand-writable, debuggable, and easy to extend with good error messages.
elements.named_in: Compilers: Principles, Techniques, and Tools (Dragon Book) - Aho, Lam, Sethi, Ullman (2006, 2nd ed.)

elements.name: Pratt Parser
elements.what: An expression parser that associates binding powers and parse functions (prefix/infix handlers) with token types, looping on precedence instead of encoding one grammar level per function.
elements.problem: Pure recursive descent needs one procedure per precedence level and deep recursion for expression grammars; driving the parse by token binding power handles arbitrary operators, precedence, and associativity in one compact loop.
elements.named_in: Top Down Operator Precedence - Vaughan Pratt (1973)

elements.name: Parser Combinator
elements.what: Parsers built as first-class functions composed by higher-order combinators (sequence, choice, repetition) so the executable parser mirrors the grammar.
elements.problem: External parser generators impose a separate toolchain and grammar language; combinators keep the grammar as ordinary host-language code, composable, testable, and extensible with custom combinators.
elements.named_in: Monadic Parser Combinators - Hutton, Meijer (1996)

elements.name: Packrat Parsing
elements.what: Recursive descent over a parsing expression grammar (ordered choice, unlimited lookahead) with per-position memoization of intermediate results, giving linear-time parsing despite backtracking.
elements.problem: Backtracking parsers can go exponential re-parsing the same input; memoizing every (rule, position) result trades memory for guaranteed linear time and lets PEGs stay composable and unambiguous.
elements.named_in: Packrat Parsing: Simple, Powerful, Lazy, Linear Time - Bryan Ford (2002)
elements.borderline: The PEG formalism itself is grammar notation (excluded as notation); packrat parsing is the implementable memoized-parsing mechanism and is kept.

elements.name: Abstract Syntax Tree
elements.what: A tree representation of parsed input that keeps semantic structure (operators, operands, constructs) while dropping concrete-syntax artifacts like punctuation and grouping tokens.
elements.problem: Later stages (analysis, interpretation, code generation, refactoring) need to traverse program structure repeatedly; a purpose-built tree decouples them from surface syntax and token order.
elements.named_in: Compilers: Principles, Techniques, and Tools (Dragon Book) - Aho, Lam, Sethi, Ullman (2006, 2nd ed.)

elements.name: Symbol Table
elements.what: A map from names to their declarations/attributes (type, storage, scope), typically organized as a stack or chain of per-scope tables to resolve lexically scoped lookups.
elements.problem: Compilers and interpreters must connect every use of a name to the right declaration under nesting and shadowing; a scoped name-to-binding structure centralizes resolution and attribute storage.
elements.named_in: Compilers: Principles, Techniques, and Tools (Dragon Book) - Aho, Lam, Sethi, Ullman (2006, 2nd ed.)

elements.name: String Interning
elements.what: Storing exactly one canonical copy of each distinct string in a pool so that equal strings share identity and comparisons reduce to pointer/handle equality.
elements.problem: Programs that handle many repeated strings (identifiers, keys, symbols) waste memory on duplicates and time on character-wise comparison; interning makes equality O(1) and deduplicates storage.
elements.named_in: Crafting Interpreters - Robert Nystrom (2021)

elements.name: Tree-Walking Interpreter
elements.what: An interpreter that executes a program by recursively traversing its abstract syntax tree, evaluating each node directly against a runtime environment.
elements.problem: Compiling to another representation costs implementation effort; evaluating the AST directly is the simplest correct execution strategy and keeps the interpreter structurally isomorphic to the language grammar, at the cost of dispatch overhead.
elements.named_in: Crafting Interpreters - Robert Nystrom (2021)

elements.name: Bytecode Virtual Machine
elements.what: An interpreter that first compiles source to a compact linear instruction encoding (bytecode) and then executes it in a dispatch loop over a virtual instruction set, usually with an operand stack or virtual registers.
elements.problem: Tree walking pays pointer-chasing and dynamic-dispatch costs on every node visit; a dense linear instruction stream improves locality and dispatch speed while remaining portable across host platforms.
elements.named_in: Crafting Interpreters - Robert Nystrom (2021)

elements.name: Threaded Code
elements.what: An interpreter code representation where the program is a sequence of addresses of operation routines, each routine jumping directly to the next, eliminating a central decode-dispatch loop.
elements.problem: A switch-based dispatch loop pays a decode branch per instruction and defeats branch prediction; threading the code through direct jumps cuts dispatch overhead and code size, historically crucial on memory-constrained machines (Forth).
elements.named_in: Threaded Code - James R. Bell, Communications of the ACM (1973)

elements.name: Panic-Mode Error Recovery
elements.what: On a syntax error, the parser discards input tokens until it reaches a designated synchronizing token (statement end, closing brace), then resumes parsing to report further errors in one pass.
elements.problem: Stopping at the first syntax error forces users into fix-one-recompile cycles, while naive continuation produces error cascades; synchronizing at stable grammar boundaries yields multiple meaningful diagnostics per run.
elements.named_in: Compilers: Principles, Techniques, and Tools (Dragon Book) - Aho, Lam, Sethi, Ullman (2006, 2nd ed.)

elements.name: Regular Expressions
elements.what: A declarative pattern notation for regular languages, compiled to a finite automaton (NFA/DFA) or backtracking matcher, used to search, validate, split, and rewrite text.
elements.problem: Hand-coding character-by-character scanning logic for each text pattern is verbose and error-prone; a compiled pattern language expresses match logic declaratively and reuses one matching engine.
elements.named_in: Regular Expression Search Algorithm - Ken Thompson, Communications of the ACM (1968)

elements.name: Event-Driven Parsing
elements.what: A parser that emits a stream of callbacks/events (start-element, text, end-element) as it consumes input, instead of materializing a full document tree.
elements.problem: Building a complete in-memory tree (DOM-style) for large or unbounded documents costs memory proportional to the document; event streaming lets consumers process input incrementally in constant memory.
elements.named_in: Simple API for XML - Wikipedia (SAX, Megginson et al. 1998)

elements.name: Pretty-Printer
elements.what: A component that renders structured data or an AST back to formatted text, choosing line breaks and indentation against a target line width using grouping/fill primitives.
elements.problem: Emitting readable text from structure requires globally consistent break and indent decisions; a layout engine over logical blocks solves this once for all output (formatters, error printers, code generators).
elements.named_in: Prettyprinting - Derek C. Oppen, ACM TOPLAS (1980)

elements.name: Read-Eval-Print Loop
elements.what: An interactive loop that reads one expression from the user, evaluates it in a persistent environment, prints the result, and repeats.
elements.problem: Batch compile-run cycles make exploration and debugging slow; an incremental read-evaluate loop with persistent state gives immediate feedback and interactive program construction.
elements.named_in: Read-eval-print loop - Wikipedia (term from the Lisp tradition)

elements.name: Escape Sequence
elements.what: Representing characters that are unrepresentable or syntactically significant in a textual context by a marker character followed by an encoded form (\n, \", <), with matching unescaping on read.
elements.problem: Embedding arbitrary text inside delimited syntax (string literals, markup, CSV) collides with the delimiters themselves; a reserved escape marker makes any character representable, at the cost of escaping the marker too.
elements.named_in: Escape sequence - Wikipedia; escape sequences defined in ISO/IEC 9899 (C standard)

elements.name: Length-Prefix Framing
elements.what: Prefixing each message or field with its byte length so a receiver knows exactly how many bytes to read, delimiting records in a byte stream without inspecting payload content.
elements.problem: Byte streams (TCP, files, UARTs) have no message boundaries; an explicit length header restores boundaries with zero payload transformation, allowing binary-transparent payloads and preallocated reads.
elements.named_in: Protocol Buffers Encoding documentation - Google (living; 'length prefixes' / LEN wire type)

elements.name: Byte Stuffing
elements.what: Framing messages with a reserved delimiter byte (e.g. SLIP END 0xC0) and escaping any payload occurrence of the delimiter or escape byte via a substitution sequence, reversed on receive.
elements.problem: A delimiter-based frame boundary breaks when the delimiter value appears in binary payload; stuffing/escaping preserves binary transparency while keeping the receiver's resynchronization trivially simple after corruption.
elements.named_in: RFC 1055 - Nonstandard for Transmission of IP Datagrams over Serial Lines: SLIP - Romkey (1988)

elements.name: Consistent Overhead Byte Stuffing
elements.what: A byte-stuffing scheme that eliminates the delimiter byte (zero) from payloads by rewriting runs as (offset-to-next-zero, data) groups, bounding framing overhead to one byte per 254 payload bytes.
elements.problem: Classic escaping can double packet size in the worst case, which breaks fixed buffer and bandwidth budgets; COBS guarantees near-constant, tightly bounded overhead regardless of payload content.
elements.named_in: Consistent Overhead Byte Stuffing - Cheshire, Baker, IEEE/ACM Transactions on Networking (1999)

elements.name: Bit Stuffing
elements.what: Inserting a 0 bit after every run of five consecutive 1 bits in payload so the flag pattern 01111110 can never occur inside a frame; the receiver removes stuffed bits.
elements.problem: Bit-level protocols (HDLC, CAN) delimit frames with a unique bit pattern and need clock-recovery transitions; stuffing guarantees the flag's uniqueness and bounds run lengths for synchronization.
elements.named_in: Computer Networks - Tanenbaum, Wetherall (2011, 5th ed.); mechanism defined in ISO/IEC 13239 (HDLC)

elements.name: Sync Word
elements.what: A known byte/bit sequence placed at the start of each frame that a receiver scans for to acquire frame (and sometimes clock) alignment in an undifferentiated stream.
elements.problem: A receiver joining or resynchronizing mid-stream has no idea where frames begin; a recognizable, low-false-positive marker sequence lets it lock onto boundaries and recover after corruption.
elements.named_in: Syncword - Wikipedia

elements.name: Type-Length-Value Encoding
elements.what: Encoding each data item as a type/tag code, a byte length, and the value bytes, so records are self-describing enough to be skipped, reordered, or extended without a shared positional layout.
elements.problem: Fixed positional layouts break when fields are added or when readers meet unknown fields; TLV lets old readers skip unknown types by length and lets messages carry optional fields sparsely.
elements.named_in: ITU-T X.690 - ASN.1 Basic Encoding Rules (BER/CER/DER); Type-length-value - Wikipedia

elements.name: Varint
elements.what: Encoding an integer in base 128 using 7 payload bits per byte with a continuation bit, so small values take one byte and the encoding is self-delimiting.
elements.problem: Fixed-width integer fields waste space when most values are small; a continuation-bit encoding sizes each value to its magnitude while still marking its own end without a length field.
elements.named_in: Protocol Buffers Encoding documentation - Google (living); LEB128 defined in the DWARF Debugging Information Format standard

elements.name: ZigZag Encoding
elements.what: Mapping signed integers to unsigned by interleaving positive and negative values (p -> 2p, n -> 2|n|-1) so small-magnitude negatives encode to small unsigned values.
elements.problem: Two's-complement negatives have all high bits set, so they encode as maximum-length varints; zigzag remaps them so varint length tracks magnitude for both signs.
elements.named_in: Protocol Buffers Encoding documentation - Google (living)

elements.name: Network Byte Order Handling
elements.what: Fixing a single byte order (conventionally big-endian) for multi-byte values on the wire or in files, with explicit host-to-wire conversion at serialization boundaries.
elements.problem: Hosts of different endianness reinterpret the same bytes as different numbers; declaring one canonical wire order and converting at the edges makes binary formats portable across architectures.
elements.named_in: RFC 791 - Internet Protocol, Appendix B: Data Transmission Order (1981)
elements.borderline: Arguably a convention plus a pair of library calls rather than a mechanism; kept because cross-endianness handling is a named, recurring design obligation in every binary format.

elements.name: Magic Number (File Signature)
elements.what: A fixed constant placed at the start of a file or message (0x7F'ELF', %PDF, 0xCAFEBABE) that identifies the format independent of names or metadata, often paired with a version field.
elements.problem: Consumers must cheaply reject wrong or corrupted inputs before parsing and dispatch on format without trusting file extensions; a distinctive leading constant provides both checks in a few bytes.
elements.named_in: Magic number (programming) - Wikipedia; List of file signatures - Wikipedia

elements.name: Schema Evolution via Field Tags
elements.what: Identifying each serialized field by a stable numeric tag rather than by position or name, so encoders and decoders built against different schema versions can skip unknown tags and default missing ones.
elements.problem: Long-lived systems must exchange data between old and new code; stable tags plus skip-by-wire-type rules give forward and backward compatibility without lockstep upgrades.
elements.named_in: Designing Data-Intensive Applications - Martin Kleppmann (2017), ch. 4 'Encoding and Evolution'
elements.borderline: Sits between a wire-format mechanism and a data-management policy; kept because the tag-and-skip mechanism is concretely implementable and named in a canonical text.

elements.name: Delta Encoding
elements.what: Storing or transmitting values as differences from a predecessor or baseline (previous sample, previous version, base frame) instead of absolute values.
elements.problem: Sequences with strong local correlation (timestamps, sensor readings, file versions) carry redundant absolute magnitude; encoding differences shrinks the representation and pairs naturally with varints and RLE.
elements.named_in: RFC 3229 - Delta Encoding in HTTP (2002); Delta encoding - Wikipedia

elements.name: Run-Length Encoding
elements.what: Replacing runs of repeated values with a (count, value) pair, the simplest lossless compression scheme designers hand-roll for run-heavy data.
elements.problem: Data with long repeats (bitmaps, sparse buffers, sensor flatlines) wastes space stored literally; counting runs compresses it with trivial, allocation-free encode/decode suitable for constrained targets.
elements.named_in: Run-length encoding - Wikipedia (technique published by Robinson and Cherry, 1967)
elements.borderline: Edge of the compression-algorithm zoo (datastructures corpus territory); kept as the one run-compression element designers routinely implement inline rather than pull as a library.

elements.name: Canonical Serialization
elements.what: Constraining a serialization format so each abstract value has exactly one legal byte encoding (fixed key order, minimal-length integers, normalized escapes), making encodings byte-comparable.
elements.problem: Signing, hashing, caching, and deduplication over serialized data break when equivalent values encode differently; a canonical form makes byte equality coincide with value equality.
elements.named_in: ITU-T X.690 - Distinguished Encoding Rules (DER); RFC 8785 - JSON Canonicalization Scheme (2020)
elements.borderline: A property imposed on a format as much as a mechanism; kept because named standards (DER, JCS) exist specifically to implement it and designers build encoders around it.

elements.name: Binary-to-Text Encoding
elements.what: Re-encoding arbitrary bytes into a restricted printable-character alphabet (e.g. 6 bits per Base64 character, with padding) so binary data can traverse text-only channels.
elements.problem: Many channels and formats (email, JSON, URLs, config files, logs) only carry text safely; mapping bytes onto a safe alphabet trades ~33% size overhead for lossless transport through them.
elements.named_in: RFC 4648 - The Base16, Base32, and Base64 Data Encodings (2006)

elements.name: Percent-Encoding
elements.what: Encoding reserved or non-ASCII octets in a URI component as a percent sign followed by two hex digits, with context-dependent reserved sets per component.
elements.problem: URIs use characters like '/', '?', '&' as structural delimiters, so data containing them corrupts the URI's own syntax; %XX escaping embeds arbitrary octets while preserving parseability.
elements.named_in: RFC 3986 - Uniform Resource Identifier (URI): Generic Syntax (2005), sec. 2.1

elements.name: Chunked Transfer Encoding
elements.what: Framing a stream of unknown total length as a sequence of length-prefixed chunks terminated by a zero-length chunk, optionally followed by trailers.
elements.problem: Length-prefix framing requires knowing the full size up front, which streaming producers cannot; per-chunk lengths plus an explicit terminator let a sender stream indefinitely while receivers still detect truncation.
elements.named_in: RFC 9112 - HTTP/1.1 (2022), sec. 7.1 'Chunked Transfer Coding'

elements.name: Serialization Proxy
elements.what: Serializing a logical snapshot object (the proxy) in place of the real object, reconstructing the real object through its public constructors on deserialization.
elements.problem: Serializing an object's physical representation bypasses constructors and invariant checks, creating fragility and attack surface; a proxy confines the serialized form to a stable logical state and re-runs validation on read.
elements.named_in: Effective Java - Joshua Bloch (2018, 3rd ed.), Item 90

parked_architecture.name: Compilation pipeline (multi-pass compiler structure)
parked_architecture.why: The lexer->parser->analyzer->codegen decomposition is a whole-program pipes-and-filters structure - system-level shape, not a single implementable mechanism; its stages (lexer, parser, AST) are cataloged as elements.

parked_architecture.name: Protocol layering / encapsulation stack
parked_architecture.why: Nesting each layer's PDU inside the next (headers-around-payload) is a system structuring principle for communication stacks; the per-layer framing mechanisms (stuffing, TLV, length prefixes) are the design-level elements.

parked_architecture.name: Interface definition language / schema-first contract (IDL)
parked_architecture.why: Generating serializers from a shared schema contract (protobuf .proto, ASN.1, CORBA IDL) is a cross-component contract-and-toolchain structure; the wire mechanisms it emits are cataloged individually.

excluded_notable.name: LR / LALR / LL table-driven, Earley, GLR parsing algorithms
excluded_notable.why: Algorithm-variant zoo (datastructures corpus territory); recursive descent and Pratt carry the design-building-block roles per the no-variant-enumeration rule.

excluded_notable.name: Shunting-yard algorithm
excluded_notable.why: A specific stack-based infix-to-postfix algorithm; the design-level role (operator-precedence expression parsing) is carried by the Pratt parser entry.

excluded_notable.name: BNF / EBNF / PEG grammar notation
excluded_notable.why: Specification notation, not an implementable mechanism; the implementable side of PEG is kept as packrat parsing.

excluded_notable.name: Parser generator (yacc, ANTLR)
excluded_notable.why: A build-time tool/practice rather than an in-program mechanism; fails the altitude test sideways into tooling.

excluded_notable.name: Interpreter and Visitor (GoF patterns)
excluded_notable.why: Canonically GoF-named; deferred to the oo-patterns scout to keep GoF names in one place (Visitor is the standard AST-traversal realization).

excluded_notable.name: UTF-8 and character encodings
excluded_notable.why: Standardized data formats rather than reusable design mechanisms; the byte-order mark is noted as an aka under magic number.

excluded_notable.name: Checksum / CRC / frame check sequence trailer
excluded_notable.why: Integral to real framing schemes but robustness-security territory (integrity checking); expected from that scout - flagged so the framing-integrity pairing is not lost.

excluded_notable.name: printf-style format strings
excluded_notable.why: Library/language feature near the raw-syntax floor; the general structured-output mechanism is covered by the pretty-printer entry.

excluded_notable.name: Off-side rule (significant indentation)
excluded_notable.why: A grammar convention (Landin 1966); its implementation is an INDENT/DEDENT tokenization variant inside the lexer element.

excluded_notable.name: Intermediate representation (IR)
excluded_notable.why: A broad compiler-internal concept spanning many concrete forms; the concrete recurring elements (AST, bytecode) are cataloged instead.

excluded_notable.name: Maximal munch (longest-match lexing rule)
excluded_notable.why: A disambiguation rule inside the lexer mechanism, not a standalone element; noted here so the name is preserved.

notes: Charter covered: all named parsing items (recursive descent, Pratt, combinators, lexer, AST, symbol table, interning, packrat/PEG, tree-walking interpreter, bytecode VM) and all named framing/encoding items (length-prefix, byte stuffing, COBS, TLV, varint, zigzag, endianness, magic number, field tags, delta, RLE, canonical serialization). Extensions beyond the charter list: threaded code (Bell 1973), panic-mode recovery, regular expressions, event-driven/SAX parsing, pretty-printer (Oppen 1980), REPL, escape sequence, bit stuffing, sync word, binary-to-text (Base64), percent-encoding, chunked transfer encoding, serialization proxy (Bloch). Axis split: 12 parsing-text, 20 serialization-framing, 2 execution-concurrency (bytecode VM, threaded code), 1 caching-memoization (string interning). Overlaps flagged: bytecode VM also in games scout charter (Nystrom); CRC/checksums left to robustness scout; GoF Interpreter/Visitor left to oo-patterns scout; null-terminated string (in-memory sentinel delimiting) assumed with the data-representation/error-handling scouts. Spot-checks this session: Oppen Prettyprinting (ACM DL), Bell Threaded Code (ACM DL), Wikipedia Syncword, protobuf encoding docs (varint/ZigZag/length-prefix naming confirmed live). Thin spots: text-processing beyond parsing (collation, tokenization for search, template engines) intentionally untouched - unclear charter ownership; compression beyond RLE/delta deliberately excluded as algorithmics zoo; no corpus works matched as naming sources (Dragon Book, Crafting Interpreters, the framing RFCs and protobuf docs are absent from work_ids.tsv - Phase 2 will need them as new nodes).
